role: Dietitian in the clinical nutrition department of a top-tier hospital
headline: A master's graduate in nutrition and food hygiene who has just passed the junior professional exam, a dietitian in the clinical nutrition department of a top-tier (Grade 3A) hospital in Nanjing, who carries a tablet round the wards every day doing nutrition risk screening, and tastes a spoonful of the diabetic meal at the hospital's diet kitchen before every service
unit: The clinical nutrition department of a top-tier (Grade 3A) general hospital in Gulou district, Nanjing (a nutrition clinic, an enteral feed preparation room and a diet kitchen; twelve staff)
level: You know nutrition risk screening, food exchange lists and enteral feed formulas by heart, and you can screen a ward on your own. In ICU consultations you can't get a word in yet, and when a clinic patient presses you, you glance at the senior dietitian
intro: The day your professional certificate came through, the department head handed you a tablet and said that from tomorrow, nutrition risk screening for general surgery and gastroenterology was yours, every new admission done within twenty-four hours. You glanced at the list: thirty-two new patients. As of today, what these patients eat three times a day, whether they can eat, and whether they're eating enough, is partly your call.
salary_note: Estimate: in a medical technology department of a Grade 3A hospital in Nanjing, a dietitian gets base pay plus performance pay, a little above the national figure for dietitians. Nutrition's performance pay usually ranks near the bottom of the hospital; only at associate chief and chief level does it catch up with doctors of the same grade.

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Joining ward rounds and consultations for complex patients, working closely with doctors to set the best nutrition therapy

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Running the nutrition clinic, seeing patients and writing diet therapy prescriptions

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 5 related job listings nationwide, 0 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: Department handover. The colleague on duty reads out yesterday's admissions who screened positive: three in general surgery, two in gastroenterology, and an old woman in oncology who has lost five kilos in three months.

To the general surgery ward. You go bed by bed with the tablet, asking each patient whether they've lost weight lately and how many mouthfuls they eat at a meal, measuring calf circumference with a soft tape, filling in the screening form. One old man says his appetite is excellent; his wife shakes her head beside him.

The enteral feed preparation room. Change, wash, cap on; you check bed number, formula and dose against each prescription, mix the feed in measuring jugs, label every bottle with the bed number and time of preparation, and send them to the wards.

Tasting at the diet kitchen before service. Diabetic meal, low-salt low-fat meal, low-protein meal, liquid diet: a spoonful of each. Today's low-salt meal includes Nanjing salted duck; you taste it and have the kitchen take it off and swap in steamed fish.

Writing nutrition records. In the electronic record system, line by line: height and weight, lab results, dietary survey, nutrition diagnosis, plan. Nine of the thirty-two need follow-up, and beside each name you note the date of the next assessment.

With the chief dietitian to an ICU consultation. A post-surgical patient's abdomen is bloated after tube feeding; the chief glances at the monitor and the fluid balance, has the pump rate halved and the formula changed. You write down why in your notebook.

Shadowing in the nutrition clinic. A woman with gestational diabetes brings her blood sugar log, and the chief teaches her to build a day's meals from food exchanges; beside them, you draw her a picture of breakfast.

Off duty. Coming out of the hospital's back gate, there's a queue at the duck-blood vermicelli soup shop by the road. Back in your rented room you open the laptop and carry on with the blood-sugar explainer the department asked you to write.

ladder.title: Dietitian (Junior)
ladder.focus: Screen and assess inpatients for nutrition risk, write nutrition records, prepare enteral feeds, taste before meals, and follow your seniors into consultations and clinics. You sit the supervising dietitian exam on accurate screening, proper records and patients who trust you.

ladder.title: Supervising Dietitian (Intermediate)
ladder.focus: Run your own nutrition clinic, take ward consultations, design enteral and parenteral nutrition plans, supervise trainees and interns, and start writing papers. You go for associate chief on the quality of your consultations, your clinic numbers and your research.

ladder.title: Associate Chief Dietitian
ladder.focus: Own a specialty area (oncology, critical care, diabetes, maternity...), lead the nutrition side of multidisciplinary consultations, run grants and supervise juniors. You go for chief on a name made in your specialty, your grants and your papers.

ladder.title: Chief Dietitian
ladder.focus: Set the department's clinical protocols and diet standards, oversee quality in the clinic and the preparation room, push screening and treatment across the hospital, and supervise graduate students and a team. You move up on building the discipline and your standing in the field.

ladder.title: Head of Nutrition Department
ladder.focus: Run the whole nutrition department's people, budget, quality control and growth, negotiate with hospital leaders and clinical departments over getting nutrition therapy onto the wards, and represent the hospital in regional quality control and professional societies. You hold the job on the department's size, quality and reputation.

ai_tasks.name: Running the nutrition clinic, seeing patients and writing diet therapy prescriptions
ai_tasks.how: AI can organize a patient's intake information, draft a diet prescription and answer common questions. The dietitian sees the patient face to face, judges in light of their condition and habits, and signs for the prescription.

ai_tasks.name: Assessing nutritional status, planning dietary requirements, writing menus and calculating nutritional value
ai_tasks.how: AI can work out nutrition needs from height, weight, lab results and requirements in moments, and generate menus and nutrient tables. The dietitian only spot-checks key cases and special groups.

ai_tasks.name: Joining ward rounds and consultations for complex patients, working closely with doctors to set the best nutrition therapy
ai_tasks.how: Rounds and consultations mean talking face to face with doctors and nurses on the ward, judging changes in a patient's condition on the spot and sharing responsibility. At most AI pulls together the materials beforehand; it can't take part in the decision.

ai_tasks.name: Inspecting, supervising and guiding meal preparation and distribution, and tasting before every service to make sure it matches the therapy
ai_tasks.how: Checking preparation and distribution on site and tasting before service depends on looking, smelling, tasting and supervising in person. AI can only help make checklists and keep records; the responsibility is a person's.

ai_tasks.name: Monitoring patients' intake, writing nutrition records, judging their metabolic state and watching the effect of nutrition support
ai_tasks.how: AI can compile intake records, draft the nutrition record automatically and flag abnormal results and trends. The dietitian judges the metabolic state, assesses how well support is working and adjusts the plan.

ai_tasks.name: Nutrition education and outreach
ai_tasks.how: AI can turn out explainers, posters, short video scripts and FAQs in bulk. The dietitian checks whether the content is scientifically sound, adapts it to the audience, and now and then gives a talk in person.

events.e_first_catch: You screened an old man who said he was "eating fine," but his calf circumference was wrong. You asked a few more questions, and his wife said he'd had only rice porridge for two weeks. Nutrition support went in, and the day he was discharged he'd gained a kilo and gave you a thumbs-up.
events.e_takeout: You set up a therapeutic diet for a diabetic patient, and the next day on the ward there was fried chicken and bubble tea on the bedside cabinet, brought in by the family. You didn't lose your temper; you sat down and talked with the family for twenty minutes, until they put the bubble tea away themselves.
events.e_ignored: You wrote nutrition consultation advice for a surgical patient, and three days later not one line had been carried out. The doctor in charge said he'd been busy and forgot. Back in the department you told the chief, and she said that's nutrition for you: you go and say it again, and again.
events.e_rumor: A diabetic patient watched a video online saying that cutting out staple foods would bring blood sugar down, went hungry until her blood sugar crashed, and was rushed to emergency. You went to see her on the ward, and the first thing she said was: that blogger sounded so sure.
events.e_exam_pass: You passed the intermediate professional exam. The day the scores came out you phoned your mother, who asked whether being a supervising dietitian means you get to be in charge of people. In charge of what patients eat, you said.
events.e_love: A young man from the clinical lab always lingered at the nutrition department door when he dropped off results. One day he asked whether dietitians eat duck-blood vermicelli after work. Yes, you said, easy on the chili oil.
events.e_ai_record: The hospital switched on a system that pulls data automatically from lab results and nursing notes and drafts the nutrition record. It saves you two hours a day, but it took the weight of a patient with edema at face value, and you caught it at a glance.
events.e_swallow: An old man with swallowing difficulties after a stroke kept choking on water. With the rehabilitation department you set him on a puréed, thickened diet, testing the thickness spoon by spoon, and two weeks later he finished a small bowl of porridge on his own.
events.e_canteen: The diet kitchen changed caterers, and in the first week every low-salt meal tasted salty. Three days running you signed the tasting sheet as failed; the kitchen manager came to the department to find you, and in the end the cook was replaced.
events.e_video: The hospital's publicity office cut a clip of you talking about blood sugar and posted it, and it passed a million views. In the comments some people praised how clearly you explained it and some called you a shill for nutrition powders. You spent the evening reading the comments, and the next day went screening as usual.
events.e_wedding: You got married. You revised the banquet menu three times, less oil, less salt; the guests said the food was quite light, and your department head said it was a nutrition department wedding.
events.e_ai_menu: The department trialed an AI menu system: enter height, weight and lab results and in seconds it produces a week's menus and nutrient tables. You checked ten cases and found it gave two kidney patients too much protein, so you added a rule to the system.
events.e_review: During the hospital's grade review, the expert panel came to the nutrition department to check screening rates and consultation records. You'd put three years of data into a stack of tables; an expert leafed to the end and asked: is this screening rate real? The chief had you take him to the wards to pick patients at random.
events.e_child: Your child was born. You were more anxious than anyone in the weaning year, calculating every spoonful of rice cereal; your mother said you grew up on rice water.
events.e_paper_reject: A paper you spent a year writing came back rejected, the reviewers saying the sample was too small. You sat in the office for a while, then opened the record system and started counting the patients you could enroll this year.
events.e_house: You put down a deposit on a flat in Jiangning, south of the city, and take the metro in to work every day. On the metro you answer nutrition clinic patients' questions on your phone, one per stop.
events.e_weight_clinic: A patient in the weight clinic stayed with you for a year, lost twenty kilos, and came off one of her blood pressure drugs. At her follow-up she wore a new dress, bought ten years ago, that she'd never been able to get into.
events.e_parents: Your father was diagnosed with diabetes. You changed the whole family's menus, and after a month he was sneaking downstairs for fried dough sticks. You had a row with him, then found him a breakfast he could eat.
events.e_mdt: At a multidisciplinary consultation led by oncology, you spoke for the first time as the person responsible for nutrition. When you'd finished, the head of surgery nodded and said from now on pre-op nutrition assessments go to nutrition first.
events.e_apprentice: A visiting trainee dietitian took her first consultation on her own and overestimated a patient's calories by a fifth. You didn't say anything in front of the patient; back in the department you worked through the formula with her again step by step.
events.e_old_patient: The granddaughter of the old man you screened years ago booked your nutrition clinic, saying her grandfather always talked about the dietitian in Nanjing who once saved him.
events.e_eyes: You find you have to hold your phone further away to read the small print on food composition tables. You got a pair of reading glasses and hung them by the computer in the nutrition clinic.

c_video.title: Do short-video health outreach or not
c_video.situation: The hospital's publicity office wants to start a short-video account for the nutrition department and wants you on camera, two videos a week. Done well it would bring patients to the clinic, but it would eat all your time after work, and the comment sections have all sorts of people in them.

options.label: Go on camera
options.result: Every Wednesday after work you talk to the camera in the department for half an hour, about putting together a breakfast and ordering takeout. Six months on the nutrition clinic is often fully booked, and patients say they saw you in the videos.

options.label: Stay off camera
options.result: You said you're more used to talking at the bedside. The publicity office found another colleague, and now and then you help her with her scripts.

c_exam.title: Sit the Supervising Dietitian exam
c_exam.situation: With a master's you can sit the intermediate exam two years after your junior title, and only once you pass can you run your own clinic and consultations. The exam months coincide with the hospital's grade review: by day you screen and write records, and at night you'd have thousands of practice questions to get through.

options.label: Sit it this year
options.result: Every night you did practice questions until midnight, working chapter by chapter through clinical nutrition, food hygiene and basic medicine. On exam day you got to the hall an hour early.

options.label: Sit it next year
options.result: You put this year's energy into the wards, and your screening and consultations got smoother and smoother. The chief said if you sit it next year you'll feel surer of yourself.

c_leave.title: Leave, or stay at the hospital
c_leave.situation: A company that makes foods for special medical purposes wants to poach you for medical affairs, offering one and a half times what you earn now; your master's supervisor is also asking whether you'd come back to the university as a lecturer. The department head says nutrition is on the way up these last few years, and short of people.

options.label: Go into medical affairs at the company
options.result: You put on a suit and travel to hospitals around the country presenting products, and every slide of your deck is full of patients like the ones you saw on the wards.
options.end: You became a medical affairs manager at a company making foods for special medical purposes, forever travelling between hospitals' nutrition departments; whenever you meet a young dietitian, you always ask how many patients they screen a day.

options.label: Go back to the university to lecture
options.result: You went back to the university to teach clinical nutrition to undergraduates, pairing every chapter with a case you'd seen on the wards.
options.end: You became a lecturer in nutrition at a university, later an associate professor; every year when you take students to the hospital for placements, you take them to the diet kitchen first to taste the diabetic meal.

options.label: Stay in nutrition
options.result: You said you hadn't had enough of the wards yet. That year the department gained another nutrition clinic room, with your name on the door.

c_ai.title: Lead the AI nutrition system or not
c_ai.situation: The IT department wants to connect nutrition screening, menus and nutrition records to AI, and wants someone from nutrition to lead it, setting the rules and checking the output with the engineers. You'd have to turn years of cases and experience into rules one by one, and answer for every mistake the system makes.

options.label: Lead it
options.result: You spent most of a year with the engineers writing in the rules for kidney, diabetic and critical care patients one by one. After the system went live, the hospital's screening rate rose from sixty percent to ninety, and you signed your name after every rule.

options.label: Don't lead it
options.result: IT found someone from another department. Once the system was out, you used it for first drafts and revised each one yourself.

c_county.title: Go to a county hospital to help build a nutrition department
c_county.situation: Your hospital partners with a county hospital in northern Jiangsu that has no nutrition department, and wants to send someone for a year to build one from nothing. You'd only get back to Nanjing at weekends, and your child is still small; when you come back and go for promotion, the posting counts in your favor.

options.label: Go to the county hospital
options.result: At the county hospital you started from an empty office, training nurses to screen and teaching the kitchen to make therapeutic diets. The day you left, the hospital director said the nutrition department sign would stay up for good.

options.label: Stay in Nanjing
options.result: You said your child was too small for you to leave. The department sent another colleague, and for a year you reviewed her records remotely.

c_senior.title: Go for Associate Chief Dietitian
c_senior.situation: Associate chief needs papers, grants, case numbers in a specialty area and a panel interview. You have two papers, a city-level grant and enough cases, but you're missing a specialty area you can really show.

options.label: Apply this year
options.result: You pulled your years of nutrition intervention for cancer patients together into a specialty area. At the panel a judge asked why you chose it, and you said because they lose weight fastest, and are most often forgotten.

options.label: Build it up two more years
options.result: You said you'd wait until the grant was finished. In those two years you were on the oncology wards even more, and your cases doubled.

c_chief.title: Go for Chief Dietitian
c_chief.situation: The senior grade looks at your weight in the field: society positions, protocols you've led, graduate students supervised, provincial grants. In the society you're only a committee member, but the in-house protocol on cancer nutrition that you led has already been taken up by several hospitals.

options.label: Apply
options.result: You gathered your years of protocols, grants and teaching one by one. At the panel a judge asked what's hardest about nutrition, and you said getting doctors to remember that patients still have to eat.

options.label: No hurry
options.result: You said a few more years. In those years you took the protocol to a dozen hospitals across the province.

c_director.title: Head of the Nutrition Department or not
c_director.situation: The old head is retiring, and the hospital director calls you in to ask whether you'll take over as head of the nutrition department. It means managing over twenty people, performance pay and quality control, and fighting the hospital for posts and space; your clinics and consultations would be cut in half.

options.label: Take it
options.result: Every week you meet hospital leaders and clinical departments, explaining why nutrition therapy has to reach every ward. The department gained a metabolic ward and a new preparation room, and your clinic went from four half-days a week to one.

options.label: Recommend someone else
options.result: You recommended another colleague in the department. You keep your clinic and your consultations, and at department meetings you sit by the door.

endings.retire: On your last day you still got to the department at quarter to eight for handover and listened to the young one on duty read out the list of positive screens. At noon you went to the diet kitchen to taste, took a spoonful of the low-salt meal, tasted it, and signed the tasting sheet for the last time. Before you left, you put the soft tape you measured calves with in the clinic drawer.
endings.burnout: In those years the department was short of people and long on work, and for months you stayed until nine every night, until one day on the ward your vision went black and you had to hold the nurses' station counter not to fall. You only heard half of what the doctor said. You applied to move to the hospital's health check center and stopped going on the wards. Later, in the advice section of the health check reports, what you wrote was longer than anyone's.

stages: Your mornings are on the wards: screening bed after bed with the tablet, asking about weight, asking about appetite, measuring calves, assessing whoever screens positive and writing it into the nutrition record; at noon you taste at the diet kitchen, and in the afternoon you prepare enteral feeds to prescription in the preparation room. In consultations and clinics you follow the chief dietitian, write down the reason for every judgment she makes, and look up the literature afterwards.

You have a nutrition clinic of your own: weight loss, gestational diabetes and kidney patients come in one by one, and with food exchanges, the body composition analyzer and a hand-drawn plate you explain how to eat a meal. You go to ward consultations on your own now, discussing enteral nutrition plans face to face with the doctor in charge; trainees and interns follow you, and in the evenings you've started writing papers.

Nutrition for cancer patients is your area now: you lead the nutrition side of multidisciplinary consultations, setting pre- and post-operative nutrition plans with surgery, oncology and radiotherapy. You have a grant and two graduate students, and Wednesday afternoons are your specialty clinic. Every new dietitian in the hospital follows you through a month of consultations first.

You set the department's rules: the screening process, the therapeutic diet standards, quality control in the enteral feed preparation room are all revised under your lead. You talk about screening rates at the hospital's quality meetings and about cancer nutrition at society podiums, and run research with your graduate students. Difficult consultations all end up with you, and after reading the record, you often go to the ward first to watch the patient eat.

The whole nutrition department is yours to run: twenty-odd people's rotas and performance pay, the quality of the clinic and the preparation room, applications for new wards and equipment. Every week you meet hospital leaders and clinical departments about getting nutrition therapy onto every ward; you represent the hospital in regional quality control and at society meetings. You have just one half-day of clinic left a week, and you never let anyone move it.
work: A pre-op patient in general surgery has low albumin on his lab results, but he says he's eating fine. You ask one more question and learn he started having diarrhea a month ago. You change the score on the assessment and mention it to the doctor in charge.

In the preparation room, the feed dose on one prescription looks wrong, half again what the patient's weight calls for. You don't make it up as written; you phone the ward, and the doctor had put the decimal point in the wrong place.

An old man on the kidney ward says the low-protein meal has no taste and won't touch it. You go to the diet kitchen and work out with the cook how to add no salt but a little more vinegar, scallion and ginger, and the next day he eats half a bowl.

A woman with gestational diabetes brings a week of blood sugar readings, high after breakfast every day. You ask what she eats, and she says a bowl of white rice porridge with steamed buns; you have her swap the porridge for a mixed-grain rice ball, and come back next week.

An ICU consultation: a critical care patient has a lot left in the stomach after tube feeding. You look at the fluid balance and the abdomen and suggest switching to feeding into the small intestine, starting low and building up; by the third day it's at half the target.

A sixteen-year-old boy comes to the weight clinic; his mother says he drinks three bottles of cola a day. You don't lecture him about calories; you have him log everything he eats on his phone for a week, and next week, in the log he brings, the cola is down to one bottle.

At a multidisciplinary consultation before stomach cancer surgery, the surgeon wants to operate quickly. You bring out the record showing the patient lost four kilos in a month and suggest two weeks of nutrition support first; the lead surgeon thinks it over and pushes the operation back ten days.

Your graduate student can never enroll enough patients for her study. You take her to the oncology ward and explain to patients and families one by one what the study is for, and that month she enrolls twelve.

A head and neck cancer patient in the middle of radiotherapy has painful swallowing and keeps losing weight. With the radiotherapy doctor you adjust the timing and thickness of his oral nutrition supplements, and teach his family a few soft dishes.

Revising the hospital's therapeutic diet standards, you change the salt in the low-salt meal from "moderate" to no more than five grams a day, and have the kitchen label every dish with its salt content.

A patient with short bowel syndrome transferred from another hospital; several hospitals' nutrition plans haven't brought his weight back. You spend three days on his records and sit through two meals with him on the ward before you settle on a new plan.

At the society's annual meeting, after you present the in-house protocol on cancer nutrition, a young dietitian from a county hospital follows you to the lift to ask if you could send her the screening form. You send it from your phone on the spot.

The hospital is discussing next year's budget, and you're fighting for a metabolic ward for nutrition. You don't talk about how important nutrition is; you bring out one table: inpatients' length of stay and costs before and after nutrition intervention.

In a quality spot check in the preparation room, one bottle's label time differs from the preparation record by twenty minutes. You don't let it go: the whole department relearns the preparation procedure, and you sign first.

Doing regional nutrition quality control for the hospital, you pick ten patients at random on a ward at a district hospital, and eight have no screening record. You don't name names at the meeting; afterwards you talk with that hospital's director alone for an hour.
past: You grew up in a housing compound in Suzhou. Your grandmother had diabetes and injected insulin every day, and from a small child you helped her check whether there was too much rice in her bowl.

In your last year of high school your grandmother went into hospital, and on the ward you saw someone from the nutrition department come on rounds for the first time: a young dietitian crouched by your grandmother's bed, asking how many mouthfuls she'd eaten that morning.

Filling in your gaokao (college entrance exam) choices, you saw "Food Hygiene and Nutrition" in a long list of majors and put it first. Your mother asked what you'd do with that afterwards. Work in a hospital, you said.

In your final year you did a placement in a Nanjing hospital's nutrition department, and on the first day followed them to screen on the wards, four wards in a morning; that night back at the dorm your feet hurt too much to sleep.

You got into a master's in nutrition and food hygiene with a supervisor in clinical nutrition. Your project was malnutrition in elderly inpatients, and in three years you screened over a thousand old people.

The year you graduated you applied to three Grade 3A hospitals' nutrition departments, and this one took you. After joining you passed the junior dietitian exam, and the day the results came out, you phoned your grandmother.

late.pension_note: Estimate: Nanjing's public institution pension plus the occupational annuity, with the hospital paying in on your full salary, so in retirement you get about 60% of your last monthly salary; being rehired for clinics brings in a separate income.
scenes: Your first week of retirement you still wake a little after seven, remember you don't have to go screening today, lie back down unable to sleep, then get up and make yourself breakfast, counting the protein.
The hospital rehires you for two half-days of nutrition clinic a week. Plenty of the people who book are ones who watched your videos years ago, coming with their children, coming with their parents.

The old folks in your compound know you're a dietitian, and on the bench downstairs they catch your arm to ask whether they can eat this, whether they can eat that. You answer one after another, and by the time you're done it's dark.
For the first few months after moving to the health check center, out of habit you still glanced into the wards as you passed, checking whether there was fried chicken on the bedside cabinets.

At the health check center you started a little talk, once a month, on how to eat your way back from the few numbers on a health check report. More and more people came; there weren't enough chairs, and some stood to listen.

An old colleague from nutrition says screening across the hospital is done automatically by the system now, and doctors call for nutrition consultations without anyone reminding them. That's good, you say, and ask whether the kitchen's low-salt meal is still salty.
For the first month after leaving the hospital, a little after eleven every day you'd glance at your watch, remembering it was time to go and taste at the diet kitchen.
The visiting trainee you supervised went back to her county hospital and built a nutrition department, and sends you a photo: the sign at the door, with her name beneath it.

The supermarket sells more and more foods for special medical purposes, the groups they're for printed on the packs. You stand at the shelf reading ingredient lists box by box, and when a young mother beside you asks which would suit an old person, you point one out.

Lots of hospitals have handed nutrition screening, menus and records to AI, which turns one out in seconds. But whether a patient actually ate, and why not, still needs someone sitting at the bedside asking.
Your own blood lipids have started running high. Dietitians are human too, you tell the family with a smile, and put one piece of braised pork back from your bowl at dinner.
When the family gathers at New Year, your grandson heaps a bowl of rice to a peak, and you reach over and push a little back, the way you used to check your grandmother's bowl when you were small.

closing.retire: One morning many years later, you make breakfast for your granddaughter in the kitchen, an egg, a little bowl of mixed-grain porridge, a few slices of cucumber, laid out on the plate like the picture you used to draw for patients in the nutrition clinic.
closing.burnout: Many years later, you sit in the sun on a bench in the compound. An old man walks past carrying a bag of fried dough sticks; you open your mouth, and in the end just smile at him.
closing.end: Many years later, sorting through old things, you find the soft tape you used to measure calves, its markings a little worn. You measure your own calf with it, glance at the number, and put it back in the drawer.
